title: Announcing Native Sandboxing in Ray | Anyscale
gist: Anyscale, in partnership with Google, ships experimental native sandboxing in Ray 2.58 built on gVisor, letting agentic-RL teams run untrusted model-generated code as ordinary Ray-scheduled resources instead of buying a hosted sandbox provider or operating a separate sandboxing system — demonstrated at 100,000 sandboxes launched in 20 seconds on GKE.

themes.theme: Sandboxing folds into the Ray stack

insights.claim: Ray 2.58 introduces native gVisor-based sandboxing (built with Google) so agentic-RL teams no longer need a hosted sandbox provider or a separately operated sandboxing system alongside their Ray cluster.
insights.speaker: Philipp Moritz, Andrew Sy Kim (Google) and Xinyu Zhang
insights.so_what: Open-source bundling of sandboxing into the dominant RL orchestration layer directly pressures standalone hosted-sandbox vendors' core use case.
insights.quote: teams building these workloads with Ray typically either rely on a hosted sandbox provider or build and operate a separate sandboxing system alongside their Ray cluster

insights.claim: Ray Sandboxing exposes two levels — a managed high-level sandbox API and low-level SandboxRuntime primitives — explicitly positioning Ray as the distributed control plane underneath custom sandbox services, supplying scheduling, autoscaling, and fault tolerance for free.
insights.speaker: Philipp Moritz, Andrew Sy Kim (Google) and Xinyu Zhang
insights.so_what: Even teams that build their own sandbox product may build it on Ray, extending Anyscale's platform gravity one layer down the stack.
insights.quote: Ray handles orchestration and scaling. gVisor handles isolation.
insights.locator: The integration is designed at two levels

insights.claim: Each sandbox is represented as a Ray Actor, so isolated environments get placement, resource reservation, failure recovery, and autoscaling through the exact APIs framework authors already use for trainers and rollout workers rather than a new abstraction.
insights.speaker: Philipp Moritz, Andrew Sy Kim (Google) and Xinyu Zhang
insights.so_what: Low integration friction accelerates adoption inside existing RL frameworks — watch how fast veRL/SkyRL-class stacks absorb it.

insights.claim: Anyscale and Google scaled Ray Sandboxing to 100,000 gVisor sandboxes created in 20 seconds across thousands of nodes on Google Kubernetes Engine.
insights.speaker: Philipp Moritz, Andrew Sy Kim (Google) and Xinyu Zhang
insights.so_what: Headline benchmark sets the bar for RL environment throughput and markets GKE as the substrate — a Google Cloud win vector for agentic-RL compute spend.
insights.quote: we have scaled this architecture to 100,000 sandboxes in 20 seconds across thousands of nodes

insights.claim: Running a separate sandbox service alongside RL training forces teams to operate a second scheduler and distributed control plane that must scale in lockstep with training; folding environment placement into Ray's scheduler eliminates that duplicate infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Philipp Moritz, Andrew Sy Kim (Google) and Xinyu Zhang
insights.so_what: The cost/complexity argument against external sandbox services strengthens as RL environment counts climb into the thousands — scale favors the integrated approach.

insights.claim: Sandbox throughput in the Harbor-on-Ray setup is typically memory-bound per node and scales horizontally via the Ray autoscaler, implying RAM (not CPU) is the binding resource for agent-evaluation fleets.
insights.speaker: Philipp Moritz, Andrew Sy Kim (Google) and Xinyu Zhang
insights.so_what: Memory-heavy instance types and memory pricing matter more than CPU for sandboxed agent workloads — relevant to cloud instance mix demand.

insights.claim: gVisor was chosen as the sandbox runtime because it reimplements much of the Linux syscall interface in userspace, giving model-generated (untrusted) code an extra isolation boundary from the host kernel while staying OCI-compatible and avoiding exposure of a Docker daemon or socket.
insights.speaker: Philipp Moritz, Andrew Sy Kim (Google) and Xinyu Zhang
insights.so_what: Confirms consensus that plain containers are insufficient for untrusted AI-generated code — isolation runtimes (gVisor-class) become standard AI-infra plumbing.
insights.quote: providing stronger isolation than executing generated code directly in ordinary containers

insights.claim: gVisor's sub-second sandbox startup and low per-sandbox memory overhead make isolated environments cheap enough to treat as fine-grained, dynamically created distributed resources rather than long-lived infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Philipp Moritz, Andrew Sy Kim (Google) and Xinyu Zhang
insights.so_what: Startup latency and per-unit overhead are the competitive axes for sandbox runtimes; microVM/appkernel vendors will be judged on these numbers.
insights.quote: gVisor also provides sub-second sandbox startup and low per-sandbox memory overhead

insights.claim: Ray Sandboxing defaults to network="none" (loopback only) with four graduated network modes and supports stripping all Linux capabilities plus OCI-spec hardening (e.g., RLIMIT_NPROC caps against fork bombs), encoding a deny-by-default security posture for agent code.
insights.speaker: Philipp Moritz, Andrew Sy Kim (Google) and Xinyu Zhang
insights.so_what: Security-by-default in open-source tooling raises the baseline buyers expect, squeezing differentiation claims of paid sandbox offerings.

themes.theme: Ecosystem hooks: RL frameworks, MCP, Harbor

insights.claim: Post-training frameworks veRL, NeMo-RL, SLIME, MILES, and SkyRL already use Ray to coordinate distributed trainers, inference engines, and rollout workers, so native sandboxing lands directly inside the incumbent runtime for LLM post-training.
insights.speaker: Philipp Moritz, Andrew Sy Kim (Google) and Xinyu Zhang
insights.so_what: Ray's entrenchment in the RL post-training stack is the distribution channel that makes this feature strategically potent for Anyscale.
insights.quote: Ray has become a common runtime for orchestrating post-training workloads.

insights.claim: Ray Sandboxes can be wrapped as an MCP tool, letting any MCP-compatible agent execute untrusted code safely with Ray and gVisor handling isolation underneath — plugging cluster-scale sandboxing into the emerging agent-tool standard.
insights.speaker: Philipp Moritz, Andrew Sy Kim (Google) and Xinyu Zhang
insights.so_what: MCP is becoming the interoperability layer through which infra vendors reach agents; sandboxed code-exec as an MCP tool is a distribution play to watch.

insights.claim: Harbor, a framework for benchmarking coding agents like Claude Code, OpenHands, and Codex CLI on SWE-Bench and Terminal-Bench, now runs natively on Ray Sandbox — on a single 14-CPU dev VM a trial takes 29s and 8 concurrent trials completed 8/8 with reward 1.0 and per-trial p50 of 45s.
insights.speaker: Philipp Moritz, Andrew Sy Kim (Google) and Xinyu Zhang
insights.so_what: Coding-agent evaluation is itself becoming an infrastructure workload; whoever hosts eval compute captures a recurring slice of agent-development spend.

themes.theme: Roadmap tells: sandbox-as-a-service, GPU sandboxes, escape-resistant configs

insights.claim: Anyscale plans a REST API so sandboxes can be consumed without Ray as a dependency and run as a standalone service on separate clusters from training — a prototyped step toward competing head-on with sandbox-as-a-service offerings.
insights.speaker: Philipp Moritz, Andrew Sy Kim (Google) and Xinyu Zhang
insights.so_what: Signals intent to commercialize beyond the Ray user base; hosted-sandbox startups should expect an open-source substitute with a service wrapper.

insights.claim: GPU-backed sandboxes are prioritized on the roadmap because workloads such as GPU kernel generation and RSI (recursive self-improvement) are described as becoming increasingly important — an unusually direct nod that self-improving-model workloads are entering infrastructure planning.
insights.speaker: Philipp Moritz, Andrew Sy Kim (Google) and Xinyu Zhang
insights.so_what: RSI named as a workload category by mainstream infra vendors is a leading indicator of where frontier-lab compute demand is heading.
insights.quote: We would like GPU-backed sandboxes to work out of the box as workloads such as kernel generation and RSI become increasingly important.

insights.claim: Anyscale plans recommended security configurations explicitly for workloads in which models may actively attempt to escape the sandbox, treating adversarial model behavior as a concrete deployment scenario rather than a hypothetical.
insights.speaker: Philipp Moritz, Andrew Sy Kim (Google) and Xinyu Zhang
insights.so_what: Containment of actively adversarial models is becoming a product requirement — a tailwind for isolation-runtime and AI-security tooling.
insights.quote: including configurations intended for workloads in which models may actively attempt to escape the sandbox
